data.title: Timeout
data.tagline: The maximum time to wait for a result before giving up and reporting failure
data.learningOutcome: You can identify whether a timeout happened during connection, sending, or response wait, distinguish it from rate limiting or a bad request, and know work may continue if the service received it.
data.description: When a save action ends in 'Request timed out', the page has reached a wait limit; this does not prove the request failed to arrive or the server crashed. Check whether the timeout happened during connection, sending, or waiting for the response, then distinguish it from rate limiting or invalid input.

learning.assumes: You have seen a page spin for a long time before failing, or a build interrupted after a long wait.
learning.outcome: You can identify whether a timeout happened during connection, sending, or response wait, distinguish it from rate limiting or a bad request, and know work may continue if the service received it.

distinctions.label: Rate limit
distinctions.explanation: A rate limit caps how many requests may run in a period and returns 429 quickly. A timeout caps how long one operation waits for a result. They are different failure causes.

distinctions.label: A malformed request
distinctions.explanation: A malformed request may get a quick 4xx response. A timeout means one waiting phase exceeded its limit; inspect the request to learn where. HTTP 408 specifically means a server timed out while waiting for the client to send a complete request message.

explanation.title: The waiting side gives up
explanation.text: When a wait phase exceeds its limit, the page or tool stops waiting and reports a timeout. If the request reached the service, work may continue there; a connection or send timeout can happen before the service receives the request.

explanation.title: A timeout is not an error verdict
explanation.text: A slow response, a busy server, or large data can all exceed the limit. The failure signal only says no result arrived; the cause still needs timing and logs.

explanation.title: Different from rate limiting
explanation.text: Rate limiting rejects too many requests per period and returns 429 quickly. A timeout means waiting a long time with no response. They need different handling.

data.boundary: Setting a very long timeout does not solve the problem: the page spins and users think it is stuck. First check whether the connection, send, or response wait timed out; then choose the limit and retry rule. Duplicate submissions can apply an action more than once.

lessonPractice.title: A form shows request timed out, but server logs show the request was processed normally and the data was written tens of seconds later. What does this show?

options.label: The client's wait limit was too short; it gave up while the server kept working
options.feedback: This example assumes the request reached the service: the page stopped waiting at its limit, but the service may have continued and written the data. The timeout alone does not prove the final result.

options.label: The server crashed halfway, so the data could not have been written
options.feedback: The logs show the request completed normally and the data was written, which contradicts a crash.

options.label: The request was never sent because the network was down
options.feedback: The server log contains this request, proving it arrived and was being processed.

data.agentPrompt: The save API sometimes takes over 10 seconds, the page reports a timeout, but the data is actually written. Find which step is slow, set a reasonable wait limit and retry rule for this request, and prevent duplicate submissions while it is still processing.
